attributes.value: On HG002 deletions, DRAGEN 4.2 with SV-informed CNV calling found 87 to 100% of deletions in every size bin, with precision 0.99 to 1.00; this is the developers' own benchmark. CNVnator matched it above 10 kb but found only 26% of deletions of 1 to 5 kb and 51% of 5 to 10 kb. On NA12878, LUMPY, DELLY and Manta recovered 88 to 94% of known CNVs, but only 20 to 33% of their calls matched; Manta and CNVnator were used to build this truth set, which can favour them. The other callers recovered 1 to 43%. Hwang et al. (2026) compared four exome callers with chromosomal microarray CNVs in 39 clinical exomes, scoring deletion and duplication exons together: sensitivity and PPV were 0.758 and 0.025 for ExomeDepth, 0.662 and 0.096 for CNVkit, 0.768 and 0.239 for CoNIFER and 0.170 and 0.041 for cn.MOPS. The truth set keeps only array CNVs with at least ten probes that overlap exome baits, so any other exon call counts as a false positive. After the authors removed regions where each tool called CNVs in more than 10% of the same 180-exome cohort, ExomeDepth reached 0.903 and 0.102 on a smaller reference set of 2,124 exons (Table 4); this filter is the authors' own method. For characterisation, Zhang et al. (2026) ran five automated ACMG classifiers on 3,031 expert-classified CNVs: five-category accuracy, averaged across classes in a way the paper does not state, ranged from 48.76% (X-CNV) to 69.81% (MarCNV-ISV) (Table 3). With likely and definite classes merged, every tool recognised more pathogenic deletions than pathogenic duplications (AnnotSV 95.16% versus 86.39%) (Table 4). Two of the three authors developed dbCNV and the reference includes their own laboratory's cases, so the dbCNV results are author-reported. None of the comparisons shown reports duplication detection separately, none covers tumour samples or long reads, and none evaluates a foundation model.

attributes.value: No study gives two reanalysis methods the same updated information and compares their new diagnoses, so this evidence cannot show which method finds more. One preprint compares methods on the same unresolved cases: in Kaschta et al. 2026, manual expert reanalysis and the automated tool Talos were applied to 219 genomes without a prior pathogenic or likely pathogenic finding. The arms had unequal inputs: the manual arm re-called the original reads with a newer DRAGEN version while Talos used the archived calls, and Talos was scored against the manual findings, so findings only Talos might have made were not counted. Each arm added the same three pathogenic or likely pathogenic cases, taking the cohort from 158 to 161 of 377 cases (42.7%), and manual reanalysis classified two new VUS cases, one of which Talos returned. Manual review took a mean of 81 minutes per case and Talos returned about three variants per case on average, but no analyst time was printed for reviewing the Talos output, so the two effort figures cannot be compared. The numbers are small, from one centre with a high initial yield, and Illumina, which makes the manual arm's software, supported the study. The other printed comparisons measure review workload, or recovery of diagnoses that were already known. In the Solve-RD CNV reanalysis of unsolved exomes, three callers returned different numbers of calls for expert review: ExomeDepth 4205, ClinCNV 2782 and CoNIFER 862. These counts overlap where callers found the same CNV, thresholds differ by caller, and ClinCNV was developed by the study's first author. In 100,000 Genomes Project cases diagnosed after a new disease-gene association, the Exomiser developers' recommended flagging rule (phenotype score increase 0.2, variant score 0.8) flagged 31 of the 37 diagnostic variants and 23 other variants, while the loosest rule tested flagged all 37 and 182 others; the rules were chosen on these same cases. In the Talos developers' ACG trio cohort, strict phenotype filtering returned 403 candidate variants instead of 487 and recovered 164 known diagnoses instead of 177. The known diagnoses come from each cohort's earlier analysis, and Talos recovery counts only diagnoses its own calling pipeline could detect. Recall on known diagnoses is not new diagnostic yield, each comparison was reported by the developers of at least one method compared, and none is clinical validation.

description: Plain-language summary of what the reviewed evidence shows. Draft until reviewed.

attributes.value: Only two sequence-only controls have been measured on the target split, both in Rewire's own runs, so there is no model comparison on it yet. On the 15,003 held-out records of the mRNABench designed-reporter test split, the composition ridge control reached a mean squared error of 1.914 against 2.366 for the training-mean control, and a Pearson correlation of 0.437; the training-mean control has no defined correlation, because its prediction is constant. The published FramePool panels are the only model comparison recorded here: neural models (FramePool and Optimus) reached Pearson 0.743 to 0.966 on the two random-sequence panels and 0.700 to 0.894 on the two human panels, while k-mer random forests, which were evaluated on the random panels only, reached 0.616 to 0.877. Those values are reported in the FramePool study on its own library, one split per panel with no uncertainty interval, and they are not measured on the designed-reporter split, so they are not baselines for it. Both Rewire controls are single runs on one split with no seed variability, and their automated audit checks the run itself, not a published score.
